Econometrician.structural_strength: The paper aligns its simulations closely with its methodological claim: it fixes the time dimension at values found in the literature survey, varies persistence and horizon, considers specifications with and without correctly chosen controls, and extends the exercise to panels and instrumental variables. This makes the Monte Carlo evidence clear evidence that conventional local-projection estimates can exhibit substantial finite-sample bias in the stated benchmark designs.
Econometrician.domain_audit: The central simulation result that local projections can be biased in short, persistent samples is supported, but the analytical characterization and proposed correction do not yet establish what the paper claims. Equation (6) is obtained by replacing the expectation of a ratio with a ratio-of-expectations approximation while omitting Taylor terms that the manuscript itself says are O(T^-1). The retained bias in equation (6) is also O(T^-1), so the omitted terms are of the same asymptotic order as the purported leading bias formula. Consequently, equation (6) is not a complete first-order bias expansion, and its sign and weighted-average interpretation need not characterize the total leading bias generally. There is also an internal sign inconsistency in Appendix A: equation (25), and therefore equation (26), adds the cross-horizon term, whereas equation (6) subtracts it, despite the statement that equation (26) nests equation (6). Finally, equation (9) is derived from the no-controls formula, while the monetary-policy application includes four lags of several controls; Appendix A indicates that controls introduce the additional matrix Psi_h, but the manuscript does not show a corresponding controls-adjusted correction. Thus, the empirical corrected responses in Figure 11 are not justified by the displayed derivation. These are repairable within the current framework, but they affect the paper's central analytical and estimator contributions.
Econometrician.best_case_contribution: The strongest credible contribution is a useful methodological warning, backed by transparent Monte Carlo evidence and a literature survey, that demeaning and finite time dimensions can produce economically large bias in local-projection impulse responses even when the observed shock is iid and even when the cross-sectional dimension of a fixed-effects panel is large. A complete bias expansion could turn the paper's cross-horizon intuition into a practical correction.
Econometrician.minimum_viable_revision: Derive the complete O(T^-1) bias expansion, including the covariance and variance terms generated by the random denominator; correct and reconcile the signs in equations (6), (25), and (26); state the assumptions under which the cross-horizon component determines the sign of total bias; and derive and implement the appropriate correction for specifications with controls before interpreting Figure 11. The revised simulations should distinguish the full analytical correction from the current partial correction and report both bias and dispersion or RMSE so readers can assess the point-estimation tradeoff.
Econometrician.severity_rationale: The Monte Carlo finding that severe bias can occur remains intact, so the paper is not fatally undermined. However, the claimed analytical bias expression omits terms of the same order as those retained, contains an apparent sign inconsistency in its controls extension, and is applied in a controlled empirical specification without a demonstrated controls-compatible correction. This places the general bias characterization, sign conclusions, proposed estimator, and empirical correction in real doubt. The problem is substantial but repairable by completing the expansion and redoing the correction within the existing framework.

novelty_claims.description: The paper claims a new analytical approximation linking finite-sample local-projection bias at one horizon to population impulse responses at other horizons, together with a transformation intended to reduce that bias.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: Section 3.2 states that equation (6) is, to the authors' knowledge, new and emphasizes the cross-horizon dependence of local-projection bias. Section 3.3 proposes equation (9), theta_BC = (I-M_T,H)^(-1) theta_LS. This is a genuine new ingredient relative to the cited autocorrelation-bias and local-projection literature, although the incomplete expansion currently limits the contribution.

novelty_claims.description: The paper documents that many published local-projection applications use substantially shorter time dimensions than those studied in the original local-projection Monte Carlo exercises.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: Section 2 surveys 71 empirical papers citing Jordà (2005), reports a median time dimension near 95, and notes that fewer than 6 percent use samples as large as T = 300 or T = 496. This is informative descriptive evidence, but it uses a Google Scholar relevance-selected sample and is primarily motivation rather than a first-order empirical discovery.

novelty_claims.description: The paper extends the finite-time-dimension bias argument to fixed-effects panels and instrumental-variable local projections, showing in its benchmark setup that increasing the number of entities need not remove bias.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: Equations (12) and (15) reproduce the same displayed cross-horizon expression as equation (6), while Figures 9 and 10 show essentially unchanged Monte Carlo bias as the number of entities rises from 10 to 50. This is a useful extension of the core argument, although its analytical force depends on repairing the incomplete first-order expansion.

insight_assessment.description: The manuscript has a clear argumentative sequence from literature practice, to benchmark simulations, to an analytical explanation, correction, extensions, and an empirical illustration. The intuition that demeaning creates dependence on responses at other horizons and that a large panel cross-section does not substitute for a long time dimension is useful. Insight falls short of HIGH because the exposition presents a partial same-order approximation as though it were the relevant bias formula, and the controls appendix does not coherently connect to the implemented empirical correction.
insight_assessment.supporting_evidence: Sections 2 through 6 follow a coherent progression, and equation (6) provides a compact organizing device. However, Section 3.2 explicitly acknowledges omitted O(T^-1) terms, Appendix equation (26) does not visibly nest equation (6) because of the opposite sign, and Section 6 applies the correction with controls without displaying the corresponding estimator.

Econometrician.layman_translation: The simulations convincingly show that local projections can miss the true response when the time series is short and persistent. The problem is that the paper's formula for explaining and correcting that bias leaves out mathematical terms that can be just as large as the terms it keeps. It also appears to reverse a sign in the appendix and then uses the simple correction in an empirical regression containing controls, even though its own appendix says controls alter the formula. The warning about bias is valuable, but the proposed general explanation and correction need to be repaired before they can be relied upon.
Econometrician.source_evidence: The key evidence is internal and direct. After equation (5), the manuscript says, "All other terms in the Taylor-series expansion are of order O(T^-1)," while equation (6)'s retained bias is itself proportional to 1/(T-h-1), hence also O(T^-1). The manuscript later concedes that its approximation "ignores some terms of the Taylor-series expansion that are of order O(T^-1)." Appendix equation (25) displays beta_h plus the weighted sum, leading equation (26) to use a plus sign, whereas equation (6) has a minus sign; the following text nevertheless says, "This expression nests the one in (6)." Equation (9) is derived from equation (7), which in turn is based on the no-controls equation (6), but Section 6 states that the empirical LPs include four lags of output growth, inflation, the federal funds rate, and the monetary-policy innovation. Appendix A shows that the controls case contains an additional Psi_h term, yet no corresponding empirical correction is derived. Figures 5 and 6 also show that the proposed correction does not eliminate the bias, consistent with it being only partial.

Theorist.structural_strength: The manuscript organizes the mechanism effectively around a simple benchmark: persistent AR(1) and AR(2) processes, an observed iid shock, and progressively richer settings with controls, panels, and instruments. This isolates the important insight that estimating each local projection separately does not make its finite-sample behavior economically or statistically independent of responses at other horizons.
Theorist.domain_audit: The basic Monte Carlo finding that persistent outcomes can generate substantial finite-sample LP bias is credible within the simulated designs, but the formal bias approximation and the proposed correction are not internally complete. First, equation (5) discards Taylor terms that the manuscript itself says are of order O(T^{-1}), while the bias retained in equation (6) is also of order O(T^{-1}). Thus equation (6) is not established as a first-order approximation to the full estimator bias without deriving or bounding those omitted ratio terms. Second, the controlled-regressor derivation contains an algebraic inconsistency: equations (23)-(24) define Psi_h through a normalized expected variance matrix inside an inverse, but equation (26) multiplies by Psi_h rather than the inverse implied by equation (23); moreover, the positive sign in equation (24) conflicts with the negative autocovariance term in equation (20). Third, equation (6) depends on responses through horizons up to T-h-1, whereas the finite matrix M_{T,H} in equations (7)-(9) simply truncates this dependence at H without an assumption or remainder bound. These issues are consequential because the empirical application includes persistent controls but applies the advertised bias correction derived from the simplified no-control mapping. The simulations can document bias, but they do not supply the missing general proof that the correction estimates the relevant bias in the controlled empirical specification.
Theorist.best_case_contribution: The strongest defensible contribution is a clear demonstration, supported by simulations and a useful demeaning-based analytic component, that LP estimates with intercepts or fixed effects can be materially biased in short, persistent time series even when the observed shock is iid, and that adding cross-sectional units need not eliminate this time-dimension bias. The paper also usefully highlights that finite-sample LP estimates are linked across horizons and proposes a computationally simple partial correction whose performance can be evaluated rather than assumed.
Theorist.minimum_viable_revision: Correct and restate the formal approximation. The authors should retain the omitted O(T^{-1}) Taylor terms or prove conditions under which they are negligible relative to the displayed term; repair equations (23)-(26) for controls; explicitly derive the controlled-regressor correction actually used in the monetary-policy application; and treat horizons beyond H as a remainder with stated assumptions or a bound rather than silently truncating them. The Monte Carlo and empirical application should then be recomputed using the corrected mapping. Alternatively, the paper could narrow the correction claim and empirical illustration to the no-control iid-regressor case while retaining the broader simulation evidence as descriptive evidence of bias.
Theorist.severity_rationale: The concern affects the paper's central claimed analytic contribution and the interpretation of its empirical bias correction, not merely exposition. Omitting terms of the same asymptotic order as the claimed bias means the displayed formula is not yet a valid leading-order characterization of total bias. The controls derivation and finite-H truncation add direct internal inconsistencies between the theory and application. Nevertheless, this is not a blocker: the central existence-of-bias result is supported by the manuscript's simulations, and the proof and correction can plausibly be repaired within the current framework by completing the expansion, fixing the matrix algebra, and rerunning the reported exercises.

novelty_claims.description: The paper claims a new analytic approximation linking the finite-sample bias of an LP coefficient at horizon h to the population impulse response at other horizons, and uses that relationship to construct a simple bias-corrected LP estimator.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: Section 3.2 states that equation (6) is, to the authors' knowledge, new and emphasizes cross-horizon interdependence; equations (7)-(9) convert that approximation into the estimator theta-hat_BC. This is a genuine new ingredient relative to the cited work on autocorrelation bias and LP interval coverage, although its current derivation is incomplete and the correction is only partial in the paper's own simulations.

novelty_claims.description: The paper documents that many published LP applications have short time dimensions and illustrates that the proposed correction can materially alter estimated monetary-policy impulse responses.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: Section 2 surveys 71 empirical papers among the 100 most relevant Google Scholar citations to Jorda (2005) and reports a median T around 95. Section 6 applies the correction to public U.S. macroeconomic data and Romer-Romer shocks. This is useful descriptive and illustrative evidence, but it uses ordinary public data, supplies no new causal identification, and is secondary to the methodological contribution.

novelty_claims.description: The paper extends the proposed finite-sample bias logic to fixed-effects panels and instrumental-variable LPs, arguing that a larger cross section need not remove bias governed by the time dimension.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: Equations (12) and (15) reproduce the no-control expression in the balanced-panel and simplified IV settings. Relating LP coefficients across horizons in these settings is a bounded but real extension, although the derivations rely on restrictive stationarity, independence, balanced-panel, and simplified instrument assumptions.

insight_assessment.description: The paper has a clear argument architecture and provides useful intuition: persistence makes distant outcomes difficult to forecast, demeaning induces finite-sample covariance distortions, and the resulting LP bias depends on responses beyond the horizon being estimated. The contrast between increasing T and increasing the panel cross section is especially illuminating. The exposition falls short of HIGH because it does not clearly separate the demeaning component captured by ratios of expected moments from the other ratio-estimator terms, and it moves too quickly from an infinite-horizon dependence result to a truncated correction.
insight_assessment.supporting_evidence: The introduction previews the simulation, analytic, panel, IV, and empirical components coherently. Section 3.2 explains why LP estimates are not truly local in finite samples, while Section 4 connects the panel result to the time dimension. However, the acknowledgment that omitted Taylor terms are O(T^{-1}) is not reconciled with the O(T^{-1}) claimed bias, and Section 3.3 offers no remainder argument for replacing the full sum in equation (6) with M_{T,H}.

Theorist.layman_translation: The paper makes a persuasive case that short samples can make local-projection responses look too small, especially when the economy is highly persistent, and that adding many countries or firms does not necessarily solve the problem. But its exact formula for how large the bias is leaves out mathematical terms that may be just as large as the terms it keeps. The formula used when control variables are present also appears algebraically inconsistent, and the proposed correction ignores responses beyond an arbitrarily selected horizon. Because the real-data example uses controls, its corrected response is not yet justified by the derivation as written.
Theorist.source_evidence: Equation (5) replaces the expectation of a ratio by a ratio of expectations. Immediately after equation (6), the manuscript concedes that the omitted Taylor terms involving variance and covariance of the numerator and denominator are O(T^{-1}); the retained expression in equation (6) is itself O(T^{-1}). Equation (6) sums j from 1 through T-h-1, but equations (7)-(9) use only an (H+1)-dimensional vector and matrix, omitting responses beyond H without a remainder term. For controls, equation (20) has a negative weighted autocovariance term, equation (24) reports the corresponding normalized matrix with a positive sign, and equation (23) places that normalized matrix inside an inverse whereas equation (26) multiplies by Psi_h directly. Finally, Section 6 states that the monetary-policy LP includes four lags of output growth, inflation, the federal funds rate, and the policy innovation, while the advertised correction in equation (9) is derived from the no-control expression.

Data_Scientist.structural_strength: The synthetic-data design is unusually transparent: the manuscript states the AR(1) and AR(2) data-generating processes, shock distributions, persistence parameters, stationary initialization, sample sizes, number of Monte Carlo replications, controls, and estimation equations. This makes the core simulation evidence conceptually reproducible and clearly separates finite-time-series bias from cross-sectional sample size.
Data_Scientist.domain_audit: The principal data-science weakness is that the hand-constructed literature-survey dataset supporting the claim that LPs are commonly used with short time series is not supplied at the observation level and uses incompletely standardized labels. The authors identify the source pool and list citations, but do not report, for each paper, the coded T, whether the panel was balanced, whether T is a mean or maximum, which specification was designated the "main LP," or how ambiguous cases were resolved. In particular, mixing mean T with maximum T creates a heterogeneous measurement whose paper-level implementation cannot be audited from Appendix C. Google Scholar's relevance-ranked sample is also nonrandom and time-varying. These limitations do not invalidate the analytic derivation or Monte Carlo result, but they leave the important representativeness claim—bias at sample sizes "commonly found" in the literature—insufficiently reproducible. The monetary-policy illustration has a related, secondary provenance gap: it gives dates and broad variable descriptions but no exact source series, vintages, aggregation rules, logarithmic transformations, missing-value treatment, or paper-ready shock file.
Data_Scientist.best_case_contribution: The strongest credible contribution is a methodological demonstration that persistent outcomes can induce substantial finite-sample bias in local-projection impulse responses even when the observed shock regressor is iid, together with an analytic approximation showing that bias at one horizon depends on the population response at many other horizons. The paper usefully extends this logic to fixed-effects panels and instrumental-variable LPs and proposes a simple partial bias correction.
Data_Scientist.minimum_viable_revision: Release a paper-level survey audit table and code containing the Google Scholar rank or inclusion source, inclusion/exclusion status, coded T, panel structure, statistic used for unbalanced panels, selected LP specification, and notes resolving ambiguity; then report sensitivity of the median and histogram to using common definitions such as median entity T, mean entity T, and maximum T. Also provide exact series identifiers, data vintages, transformations, aggregation procedures, missing-data rules, and the monetary-shock file or reconstruction code for the empirical illustration. No redesign of the theoretical or simulation framework is required.
Data_Scientist.severity_rationale: The undocumented and heterogeneous survey labels directly support a recurring motivational claim that the simulation sample sizes are representative of empirical practice. If alternative coding of unbalanced panels, the "main LP," or the relevance-ranked source pool materially changes the distribution of T, the manuscript must narrow its claim about how common the problem is. The analytic existence of finite-sample LP bias would remain intact, so this is not a blocker; it is a repairable data-construction and reproducibility defect within the current framework.

novelty_claims.description: Derives an analytic approximation linking finite-sample bias in an LP coefficient at horizon h to the population impulse response across other horizons, and uses that relationship to construct a simple bias-corrected estimator.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: Section 3.2 presents equation (6), while Section 3.3 rewrites the approximation as a system and defines the correction in equation (9). The manuscript explicitly relates the derivation to established autocorrelation-bias work by Kendall (1954) and Shaman and Stine (1988), so this is a genuine but bounded extension of known finite-sample-bias logic rather than an entirely new estimation paradigm.

novelty_claims.description: Shows that the same approximate LP bias survives fixed-effects panel estimation and a stylized instrumental-variable formulation, including cases where increasing the panel cross-section does not reduce bias.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: Equations (12) and (15) reproduce the same approximate bias expression as equation (6), and Figures 9 and 10 show essentially unchanged Monte Carlo means as the number of entities rises from 10 to 50. This is a useful extension to empirically important implementations of LPs.

novelty_claims.description: Constructs a survey of prominent papers citing Jordà (2005) and reports that the median time dimension is approximately 95, much shorter than the sample sizes in Jordà's original Monte Carlo exercises.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: Section 2 states that 71 of the 100 most relevant Google Scholar results used LPs and reports a median T around 95. The underlying publications are public and the contribution is descriptive; moreover, paper-level coding is not included, limiting the evidentiary novelty and auditability of the resulting distribution.

insight_assessment.description: The paper has a clear argument architecture: document short empirical samples, demonstrate bias in transparent benchmark processes, derive a cross-horizon explanation, propose a correction, and extend the result to panels and IV. The explanation that finite-sample LP estimates are not truly "local" because their biases depend on responses at other horizons is particularly useful. The presentation is generally effective, though the empirical-data lineage and the interpretation of the survey's representativeness need greater precision.
insight_assessment.supporting_evidence: Equation (6) directly motivates the cross-horizon interpretation, Figures 2 through 4 connect the approximation to simulation evidence, and Sections 4 and 5 preserve the same logic in panel and IV settings. Section 6 also explains how long-horizon coefficients affect the monetary-policy correction rather than reporting the adjusted curves mechanically.

Data_Scientist.layman_translation: The paper convincingly shows, using formulas and simulations, that local projections can understate persistent economic responses when the time series is short. However, its claim that such short samples are typical relies on a manually coded literature survey whose paper-by-paper measurements and decisions are not shown. Publishing that audit trail and the exact macroeconomic data construction would make the empirical motivation and illustration reproducible without changing the main method.
Data_Scientist.source_evidence: Section 2 says the authors examined the 100 "most relevant" Google Scholar papers, retained 71 empirical applications, and for unbalanced panels used "the mean T across entities, when readily available, or ... the largest value of T across entities." It also refers ambiguously to "the main LP" without an operational selection rule. Appendix C lists publications but does not pair them with coded T values or coding notes. Section 6 identifies quarterly data from 1969:Q1–2008:Q4, "real output growth," "annualized inflation," and the Romer-Romer shock extension, but does not provide exact series identifiers, vintages, transformation formulas, aggregation rules, or missing-data procedures. By contrast, Sections 3 and 4 explicitly provide the simulation DGPs, iid normal shocks, rho and psi values, N = 10,000, candidate T values, controls, and stationary initialization.

Econometrician.referee_acknowledgment: The reviews converge on a serious but repairable problem: the simulations credibly demonstrate finite-sample bias in the benchmark designs, while the displayed analytical approximation and correction do not yet justify the paper's general theoretical and empirical claims.

attacks.critique: The survey documentation problem is real, but classifying it as a severity-5 substantive flaw overstates its damage to the paper. The survey motivates the selected sample sizes; it is not needed to establish the Monte Carlo existence result or the analytical mechanism. The claim that the chosen sample sizes are broadly representative should be qualified and supported with a coding table, but the central methodological result survives even if that descriptive claim is narrowed.
attacks.evidence: Sections 3 through 5 specify and analyze T = 50, 100, and 200 independently of the literature survey. Section 2 supplies motivation for calling these empirically relevant values, but no later derivation depends on the reported median T of approximately 95. The missing paper-level coding therefore affects reproducibility and representativeness of the survey, not the existence of finite-sample LP bias.

defenses.argument: A paper-level coding table, exact empirical series identifiers, transformations, and reconstruction code would materially improve reproducibility. Nevertheless, these omissions do not invalidate the transparent synthetic-data results, and the monetary-policy exercise is explicitly illustrative rather than a new identification result. They should not be treated as the principal publication barrier.

concessions.reason: I agree that the paper omits Taylor terms of the same O(T^-1) order as the displayed bias component, truncates cross-horizon dependence at H without a remainder argument, and does not coherently derive the controls-adjusted correction used in the empirical application. These defects directly undermine the claimed general bias formula and estimator, although they are repairable within the existing framework.

questions.question: Would you regard the paper as technically adequate if it explicitly relabeled equation (6) as only the demeaning-induced component of bias, restricted the proposed correction to that component, and removed the controlled empirical correction, or do you view a complete O(T^-1) expansion as necessary for any publishable analytical contribution?

Would qualification of the representativeness claim plus release of the paper-level survey coding table reduce your concern to a minor reproducibility issue, given that the simulation and theoretical conclusions do not depend on the estimated median T?

Econometrician.final_argument_state: The surviving execution assessment is mixed. The literature survey and Monte Carlo designs provide credible evidence that conventional LP estimates can exhibit economically large finite-sample bias in short, persistent samples, including fixed-effects panels where increasing the cross-sectional dimension does not remove time-dimension bias. However, the central analytical contribution is not yet sound: equation (6) retains one O(T^-1) component while omitting other O(T^-1) ratio-estimator terms; the manuscript contains unresolved sign or matrix inconsistencies in the controls derivation; the finite-H correction lacks a treatment of omitted longer-horizon responses; and the monetary-policy application uses controls without deriving the corresponding valid correction. Novelty remains MEDIUM because the cross-horizon characterization and panel/IV extensions are potentially useful if repaired. Insight remains MEDIUM because the demeaning and cross-horizon intuition is clear, but the manuscript fails to distinguish a partial bias component from a complete leading-order expansion. The survey's representativeness and data-provenance language also require narrower claims and better documentation, but these are secondary. A complete first-order derivation, corrected controls implementation, truncation analysis, and revised simulations reporting bias and RMSE can salvage the paper within its current framework.

Theorist.referee_acknowledgment: The graph converges on the correct decision: the simulations credibly establish finite-sample bias in the stated benchmark designs, but the manuscript does not yet establish its advertised leading-order bias formula or the correction used in the controlled empirical application. The Econometrician's audit most directly identifies the decision-relevant defects, while the Data Scientist adds useful but secondary reproducibility concerns.

attacks.critique: The proposed minimum viable revision is materially incomplete because it says no revision of the theoretical framework is required. Releasing survey coding and empirical-data documentation would improve reproducibility, but it would not repair the central analytical problem: the manuscript omits Taylor terms of the same order as the displayed bias, truncates responses beyond H without a remainder argument, and applies a no-controls correction to an application with controls.
attacks.evidence: Section 3.2 acknowledges that omitted ratio-expansion terms are O(T^-1), the same order as equation (6). Equation (6) involves responses through T-h-1, whereas equations (7)-(9) retain only horizons through H. Section 6 includes four lags of several controls, although equation (9) is derived from the no-controls mapping. Thus data documentation alone cannot make the central correction theoretically valid.

attacks.critique: The survey reproducibility gap is real, but characterizing it as the principal data-science weakness should not obscure that it mainly affects the motivational claim about how common short-T applications are, not the validity of the transparent Monte Carlo demonstration conditional on chosen T. Its decision relevance is therefore secondary to the estimator derivation.
attacks.evidence: The Monte Carlo DGPs, sample sizes, persistence parameters, controls, initialization, and replication count are stated directly in Sections 3 and 4. By contrast, the missing paper-level survey table affects the interpretation of the median T and representativeness of the literature survey, rather than generating the simulated bias itself.

defenses.argument: The Econometrician's classification of the omitted same-order Taylor terms as a substantive flaw is justified rather than an excessive demand for refinement. Because both the retained demeaning component and the omitted random-denominator components are O(T^-1), the manuscript cannot call equation (6) the operative leading bias expression or infer the sign of total leading bias without calculating or restricting the omitted terms.

concessions.reason: I agree that the empirical correction is unsupported as presented. Equation (9) follows from the no-controls mapping, whereas the monetary-policy regressions contain multiple persistent controls; the appendix signals additional control-dependent matrices but the manuscript does not derive and implement the corresponding correction coherently.

I agree that the literature survey and monetary-policy application are not fully auditable from the manuscript. A paper-level coding table and exact series, transformations, vintages, and shock-construction files are warranted, although these are secondary to the analytical defect.

Theorist.final_argument_state: The surviving execution assessment is mixed. The literature survey is informative but incompletely reproducible, and the Monte Carlo evidence is transparent and persuasive for the benchmark claim that conventional LP estimates can be materially biased in short, persistent samples. The central analytical contribution is not yet sound: equation (6) retains only one O(T^-1) component while omitting other O(T^-1) ratio terms; the controls derivation is internally inconsistent; the finite-H correction lacks a tail remainder or identifying restriction; and the empirical application uses controls without a justified controls-adjusted correction. Novelty remains MEDIUM because the cross-horizon bias mechanism, panel/IV extensions, and proposed transformation are genuine bounded contributions if repaired. Insight remains MEDIUM because the paper clearly explains why finite-sample LP behavior is not local and why increasing the panel cross section need not substitute for increasing T. The issue is not primarily rephrasing: the proof and implementation require substantive revision within the existing framework. The appropriate verdict is RESUBMIT.

Data_Scientist.referee_acknowledgment: The econometric and theoretical reviews identify a more consequential defect than the reproducibility limitations emphasized in the data-science review: the displayed approximation omits terms of the same asymptotic order as the retained bias component, and the empirical correction is not derived for its controlled specification. The transparent simulations remain informative about finite-sample bias, but they do not validate the proposed correction as a complete first-order procedure.

attacks.critique: The alleged sign inconsistency involving Appendix equations (25) and (26) cannot be audited from the supplied manuscript because the provided Appendix A ends during the derivation following equation (20). This allegation should be removed or explicitly marked as unverifiable from the available content. The independently visible same-order omission and controls-application problems remain valid.
attacks.evidence: The supplied manuscript includes Appendix equations (16) through (20) and then truncates mid-expression. Equations (25) and (26), quoted in the review graph, do not appear in the manuscript content available for this audit.

attacks.critique: The detailed claims about the algebra of Appendix equations (23) through (26), including the placement of Psi_h and the asserted sign conflict in equation (24), exceed the supplied evidence. Those equations are absent from the provided manuscript excerpt, so this portion of the critique is not independently supportable here. The objection to omitted O(T^-1) terms and the unexplained truncation at H is nevertheless supported by the visible main text.
attacks.evidence: Appendix A is truncated shortly after equation (20). Consequently, equations (23) through (26) and the definition of Psi_h cited by the review are not present in the supplied manuscript.

concessions.reason: I concede the central mathematical objection. The manuscript explicitly states that the omitted Taylor terms are O(T^-1), while the retained expression in equation (6) is itself O(T^-1). Therefore equation (6) is not shown to be the complete leading-order bias, and its sign interpretation and correction require additional derivation. I also concede that equation (9) is derived from the no-controls mapping whereas Section 6 applies a correction to LPs containing several lagged controls without displaying the corresponding controlled-regressor correction.

I concede the horizon-truncation problem. Equation (6) involves responses through T-h-1, but equations (7) through (9) construct a finite system through H without a tail assumption, remainder bound, or sensitivity theory. Because the manuscript itself explains that long-horizon responses can materially affect short-horizon corrections, this omission is consequential rather than cosmetic.

questions.question: After including all O(T^-1) ratio-estimator terms, under what restrictions, if any, would the displayed cross-horizon component still determine the sign of total leading bias?

Would you regard a revision that explicitly labels equation (9) as a partial demeaning-bias adjustment, rather than a first-order bias correction, as adequate if it also reports RMSE and tail-horizon sensitivity?

Data_Scientist.final_argument_state: The surviving execution assessment is mixed. The Monte Carlo design is transparent and supports the narrower descriptive result that conventional LP estimates can have economically large finite-sample bias in the specified persistent AR benchmarks, including fixed-effects panels where increasing the cross section does not increase the time dimension. The literature survey and monetary-policy data remain insufficiently reproducible because observation-level coding, exact series provenance, transformations, and reconstruction code are not supplied. More importantly, the proposed analytical correction is not established as a complete first-order correction: the manuscript omits Taylor terms of the same O(T^-1) order as the retained component, truncates cross-horizon dependence without a remainder argument, and applies the no-controls correction to an empirical specification with controls without presenting the appropriate mapping. Novelty remains MEDIUM because the cross-horizon bias perspective and panel/IV extensions are potentially useful, but their formal contribution is conditional on repair. Insight remains MEDIUM: the finite-sample nonlocality intuition is clear, while the distinction between a partial demeaning component and total estimator bias is not. The paper needs substantive within-framework revision, recalculated simulations and application results, and improved data provenance; rejection is unwarranted because the core simulation evidence and conceptual mechanism remain salvageable.

Econometrician.referee_acknowledgment: The review graph correctly converges on RESUBMIT: the benchmark simulations establish a meaningful finite-sample phenomenon, but the proposed analytical correction is not yet a complete leading-order bias correction. I also accept the Data Scientist's evidentiary limitation that alleged inconsistencies in unavailable Appendix equations cannot be maintained from the supplied manuscript.

attacks.critique: The instrumental-variables extension treats the finite-sample expectation of a just-identified ratio estimator as well defined without assumptions ensuring that this expectation exists. The sample covariance in the denominator can approach or cross zero, so the IV estimator can have heavy tails or undefined moments. Consequently, equations (14)-(15) do not establish that finite-sample IV bias is identical to the OLS expression.
attacks.evidence: Equation (13) defines the scalar IV estimator as cov-hat(z_t,y_{t+h}) divided by cov-hat(z_t,epsilon_t). Section 5 imposes validity and serial-independence conditions but no distributional, first-stage, or moment-existence condition that bounds the random denominator away from zero. It then directly invokes E[theta-hat_IV] in equation (14).

final_report.editorial_rationale_and_integration:
Decision: MAJOR REVISION REQUIRED. The strongest credible version of the paper makes a useful methodological point: in the stated persistent, short-T designs, conventional local projections can exhibit economically important finite-sample bias even with an iid observed shock, and increasing the cross-sectional dimension of a fixed-effects panel need not remove bias driven by the time dimension. The Monte Carlo designs are transparent and support this narrower result. The paper also offers a promising intuition that finite-sample LP behavior is not genuinely local because estimates at one horizon are connected to responses at other horizons. Novelty and insight are both best assessed as MEDIUM: the cross-horizon perspective, proposed transformation, and panel and IV extensions are potentially useful, but they are bounded extensions whose formal validity remains incomplete.

The decisive concerns are substantive rather than presentational. First, equation (6) is used as the operative bias mapping even though the manuscript states that omitted variance and covariance terms from the ratio expansion are O(T^-1), the same order as the retained component. The paper therefore has not established equation (6) as the complete leading-order bias, nor shown that its displayed component determines the magnitude or sign of total first-order bias. Monte Carlo proximity in selected designs cannot replace deriving or bounding the omitted terms. Second, equation (6) depends on responses through T-h-1, while equations (7)-(9) retain only horizons through H. No tail assumption, truncation remainder, or sensitivity bound justifies this finite-dimensional inversion, despite the empirical discussion emphasizing that distant responses can materially affect short-horizon corrections. Third, the implementable correction is derived for the no-controls case, but the monetary-policy LP includes four lags of several variables. The supplied manuscript does not complete and implement a corresponding controls-adjusted mapping, so the corrected empirical responses are not justified by the displayed theory. Fourth, the IV section invokes the finite-sample expectation of a ratio estimator without conditions ensuring existence of that expectation or controlling a denominator that may approach zero; instrument strength, moment existence, and the additional ratio terms require treatment.

There is no unresolved blocker and the benchmark simulation finding remains intact, so these problems do not warrant rejection. They do, however, affect the central analytical, estimator, extension, and empirical claims and require a genuine resubmission. Specific allegations about signs or matrices in appendix equations unavailable in the supplied manuscript are not relied upon here. There is likewise no separate substantial-rephrasal issue: the central problem is mathematical validity, not merely wording. Minor rephrasal and reproducibility issues remain. Claims that the selected T values are representative of the literature should be calibrated because the survey uses a relevance-ranked, nonrandom source pool and heterogeneous coding of unbalanced panels. The paper should provide observation-level survey coding and exact empirical-data provenance and replication materials. These documentation issues affect representativeness and auditability, not the existence of bias in the stated simulations. Inference, optimal selection of H, and broader DGPs may remain future work; they are not prerequisites beyond what is needed to validate the paper's present claims.
final_report.official_letter_to_the_author:
Dear Authors,

The paper addresses an important practical question and has a credible core result. Your transparent simulations show that conventional local-projection estimates can be materially biased in short, persistent samples, including settings with an observed iid shock. The panel exercises also clearly illustrate that adding cross-sectional units need not eliminate bias governed by a fixed time dimension. The accompanying intuition—that finite-sample LP estimates at different horizons are linked—is promising and could support a useful methodological contribution.

I am inviting a major revision because the analytical characterization and proposed correction do not yet establish the claims placed on them. The principal issue is equation (6). The manuscript acknowledges that the omitted variance and covariance terms in the Taylor expansion are O(T^-1), while the component retained in equation (6) is also O(T^-1). As written, equation (6) is therefore not shown to be the complete first-order bias expansion. It may identify an informative demeaning-induced component, but the paper cannot infer the magnitude or sign of total leading bias, or describe equation (9) as a first-order correction, without deriving the remaining terms or imposing and defending conditions under which they are negligible. The simulations show that the partial expression can approximate bias in selected designs, but they do not supply the missing general argument.

A second issue is truncation. Equation (6) links bias at horizon h to responses extending through T-h-1, whereas equations (7)-(9) form a system only through a chosen H. The revision must state an explicit tail restriction, derive a truncation remainder or bound, or otherwise provide a defensible extrapolation and sensitivity analysis. This is especially important because the empirical discussion itself emphasizes that responses beyond the displayed horizons can materially alter the correction.

Third, the empirical application estimates LPs with four lags of output growth, inflation, the federal funds rate, and the policy innovation, while the displayed correction is derived for regressions without controls. Please derive the correction for the exact controlled specification and explain precisely how it is implemented, then recompute the application. If that derivation cannot be supplied, the defensible alternative is to restrict the correction claim and application to settings covered by the theory and present the controlled simulations only as descriptive evidence of bias.

Fourth, the IV extension requires additional foundations. Because equation (13) is a ratio with a random sample covariance in the denominator, please state conditions governing instrument relevance, denominator behavior, and moment existence before invoking its finite-sample expectation. The same-order ratio-expansion terms must also be incorporated or the IV claim narrowed accordingly.

After repairing the theory, please rerun the relevant simulations and empirical exercise. Report not only mean bias but also dispersion or RMSE, so readers can assess whether the correction improves point-estimation risk rather than only moving the mean. Clearly distinguish a complete analytical correction from any partial adjustment.

The remaining issues are secondary but should be addressed. Please release a paper-level survey table recording inclusion decisions, coded T, panel structure, the statistic used for unbalanced panels, the selected LP specification, and ambiguity notes. Report sensitivity to alternative definitions of T and qualify claims of representativeness as appropriate. For the monetary-policy illustration, provide exact series identifiers, vintages, transformations, aggregation and missing-data rules, the shock series or reconstruction procedure, and replication code. These changes are needed for auditability, although they do not undermine the transparent benchmark simulations.

The revision should preserve the paper's strongest contribution rather than overstate it: a well-supported warning about finite-sample LP bias and a rigorous account of the cross-horizon component. If the complete expansion, tail treatment, controls implementation, and IV conditions can be supplied, the proposed correction could become a meaningful contribution. If not, the paper should narrow its estimator claims and present the current mapping explicitly as a partial adjustment.

Sincerely,
Senior Coordinating Editor

final_report.constructive_summary: The paper has a viable and useful core: transparent simulations demonstrate substantial finite-sample LP bias in short, persistent benchmark designs, and the panel results clarify why a large cross section does not substitute for a long time dimension. Its most promising conceptual contribution is the cross-horizon interpretation of finite-sample bias. The present manuscript does not yet validate its advertised analytical formula or correction because it omits same-order Taylor terms, truncates the horizon mapping without controlling the tail, applies a no-controls correction to a controlled empirical specification, and leaves the IV ratio expectation insufficiently founded. These are serious but repairable within the existing framework. A successful revision should either complete the theory and recompute the evidence or narrow the estimator claim to a clearly labeled partial adjustment, while also improving survey and empirical reproducibility.
